items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the City Club of Cleveland, 'It Takes Two to Make an Economy Go Right'
items.quote: But if recent trends continue, it may soon be appropriate to act.
items.summary: Hammack said holding rates steady is reasonable for now given uncertainty, but inflation is too high and moving higher and policy may not be sufficiently restrictive. She is more concerned about persistently elevated inflation than about employment, and said more restrictive policy could well be needed. She noted financial conditions are supportive, with large technology companies funding capital spending at favorable rates and spreads.
items.score_note: Supports holding today but signals a hike may soon be appropriate and that policy may not be restrictive; lean tighter, not yet an explicit call to raise.
items.ai_quote: Some of the largest technology companies have funded their capital investments at favorable interest rates and attractive credit spreads.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Interview with Yahoo Finance
items.quote: Monetary policy is exactly in the right place.
items.summary: Williams said he sees no need to raise or lower rates right now and no obvious direction for where rates would go next. Reuters' account of the same interview adds that he viewed the energy price rise as a one-time effect.
items.score_note: Explicitly neutral: no need to move in either direction and no obvious direction ahead.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Prepared remarks for Crane's Money Fund Symposium (not delivered; text published on NY Fed Teller Window at the scheduled time)
items.quote: The current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to do that.
items.summary: Williams said inflation is unquestionably elevated but should edge down as tariff effects fade and energy prices stabilize; the June hold at 3.50-3.75% leaves policy well positioned. He forecast inflation at 3.5% by year-end and 2% in 2028, and described the ample-reserves framework and the reduction of reserve management purchases to $10B a month.
items.score_note: Endorses the hold and calls the stance well positioned; no lean toward hiking or cutting.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview on CNBC from the ECB Forum in Sintra, Portugal
items.quote: we may need to raise rates to bring that policy restraint in and to bring inflation back down
items.summary: In her first comments after the June FOMC, Hammack said inflation has been too high for five years and that if it persists without policy restraint, rates may need to rise. She cited insatiable hyperscaler demand for data-center inputs as a price pressure and said neither borrowing costs nor credit conditions are discouraging business investment. Reuters reported she declined to say when the threshold for hiking would be met.
items.score_note: Open to hiking if inflation persists; conditional rather than a call to raise now.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Interview on Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria'
items.quote: Right now, I think policy is in a good place.
items.summary: Williams said inflation is still too high but he feels somewhat more positive about the near-term outlook because of expected energy price declines. He said monetary policy is well positioned and what comes next depends on the data; he gave no guidance on whether the next move is up or down. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Policy 'in a good place', data dependent, no directional lean.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Q&A at a conference hosted by the New York Fed
items.quote: I do think monetary policy is, and continues to be, well positioned
items.summary: Williams said AI-driven demand is the inflation driver he is most focused on: if it creates a sustained impulse to demand relative to supply, policy would not look through it and would need to respond. If things play out more benignly, policy remains well positioned. Core PCE of 0.2% a month in the second half would be consistent with continued disinflation. Reuters reported he declined to say what he would do at the July meeting and expects energy prices to come down.
items.score_note: Baseline is that policy is well positioned; the tightening scenario is conditional on persistent AI-driven inflation. Torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the Partnership for New York City, 'Stability of Thy Times'
items.quote: The current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to do that.
items.summary: Williams said inflation at about 4% is unquestionably too high, driven by tariffs, Middle East energy disruptions and AI-related demand, but he sees reasons it has peaked. He backed the mid-June hold, forecast inflation near 3.25% by year-end and 2% in 2028, and said his views will follow the totality of the data.
items.score_note: Explicitly says the current stance is well positioned after the June hold; data dependent with no stated lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on the last day before the July FOMC blackout
items.quote: The labor market is right around my level of maximum employment.
items.summary: Hammack wrote that there is no conflict in the mandate: inflation is too high and broad-based while the labor market is around maximum employment, so persistently high inflation is the bigger concern. Other coverage of the post quotes her saying businesses now tell her the Fed needs to act to curb inflation.
items.score_note: Inflation risk clearly dominates and sets up her July dissent, but the post itself stops short of calling for a hike.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: FOMC meeting of July 28-29, 2026: dissent in favor of a 25bp increase (with Kashkari and Logan)
items.quote: Voting against the monetary policy action were Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate
items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3.50-3.75%. Hammack, Kashkari and Logan voted against, preferring a 1/4 percentage point increase at this meeting. The quote is the vote line of the FOMC statement, not Hammack's own words.
items.score_note: Formal dissent in favor of a rate increase.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Written statement explaining her dissent at the July 28-29 FOMC meeting
items.quote: I preferred to move at our recent meeting because I did not see the current policy stance as appropriately restrictive.
items.summary: Hammack said she dissented in favor of raising the federal funds rate because inflation has been too high for too long and she is not confident it will return to 2% on its own. She sees demand-side as well as supply-side pressure, a labor market near maximum employment, and said now is the time for the FOMC to act.
items.score_note: Explains a dissent for a hike and says now is the time to act.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Interview with Reuters (conducted July 31, transcript published August 3)
items.quote: it would absolutely be appropriate to act to get us on a trajectory that does bring inflation back to 2%
items.summary: Two days after the July hold (which he strongly supported while three colleagues dissented for a hike), Williams said policy is well positioned to support the disinflationary path he expects in the second half and next year. If the economy is not on a trajectory back to 2%, acting would be appropriate. On AI he said debt financing is rising but, given high earnings, he is not as worried about financial stability from leverage right now. The New York Fed posted its own takeaways on August 3.
items.score_note: Defends the hold and calls policy well positioned; willingness to hike is conditional on inflation failing to fall.
items.ai_quote: so I'm not as worried about the financial stability from the leverage right now

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Essay 'Monetary Policy Perspective: Keeping an Open Mind' published on the Philadelphia Fed site
items.quote: If instead underlying inflation remains stubbornly elevated, the passage of time without progress would itself signal that more restrictive policy is needed.
items.summary: Paulson said she supported the July hold and is keeping an open mind between two scenarios: policy is mildly restrictive and will return inflation to 2%, or it is not restrictive enough. Underlying inflation is 2.4-2.8% and has edged down only modestly; ready credit access is supporting robust AI investment and price pressure. She will judge by how evidence accumulates.
items.score_note: Backs the hold but openly entertains that policy is not restrictive enough and that lack of progress would call for tightening; open to hiking without calling for it.
items.ai_quote: Many firms have ready access to credit, and this is supporting robust investment, especially in AI.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview on CNBC 'Squawk Box' with Steve Liesman
items.quote: If we don't see that progress, then we have to be open to recalibrating monetary policy
items.summary: Paulson said the July hold was not a close call for her: policy needs to be mildly restrictive and she thinks it has been. Underlying inflation is 2.4-2.8% and she needs to see progress from here; without it the Fed must be open to recalibrating, which could mean higher rates or the same rates for longer. She said she has an open mind on Chair Warsh's proposal to change the meeting schedule.
items.score_note: Hold was clear-cut and policy judged mildly restrictive; tightening is conditional. Scored one notch nearer zero than her same-day essay, which gives more weight to the not-restrictive-enough scenario.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview with Yahoo Finance
items.quote: I think that now is the time for us to start acting, to start bringing more restraint into policy
items.summary: Hammack said one 25bp move probably does not do much, so some number of increases is likely needed, though she would not prejudge how many. She said the 3.50-3.75% range is not meaningfully restricting the economy, businesses report no restraint on investment, and the weak July jobs report did not change her view because unemployment at 4.1% is near full employment.
items.score_note: Explicit call to start raising rates now and for more than one hike.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the Dayton Area Chamber of Commerce, Ohio
items.quote: I think that we need to act now because I think we need to bring inflation back down to that 2% objective faster
items.summary: Hammack reiterated that the Fed should raise rates now. She said businesses are excited to borrow and invest, so policy needs some restraint to get inflation from above 3% to 2%, and that two months of better inflation data do not give her confidence. She questioned whether taking another three or four years to reach 2% is acceptable. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Explicit call to act now.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview on Fox Business Network during Jackson Hole week
items.quote: My forecast is that inflation is going to end this year around 3%
items.summary: Hammack said inflation will end 2026 around 3% and reach maybe the mid-twos at best next year, so the Fed will not be back at target even by next year. Reuters reported that she reiterated her belief that a rate hike is needed. Other outlets attribute similar same-week remarks to CNBC and Bloomberg interviews (see unverified).
items.score_note: The direct quote is a forecast, but Reuters reports in the same piece that she reiterated a rate hike is needed, consistent with her dissent and her August 10 and 13 remarks.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Interview on CNBC
items.quote: depend on the data and depend on some of the risks to achieve our goals
items.summary: Ahead of the September 15-16 meeting, Williams said the decision will depend on the data and the risks, and that there is no clear science saying policy is in the right position. He attributed the rise in long-term yields to a strong economy fueled by investment in AI and data centers rather than inflation fears, and called recent inflation data encouraging but not yet enough. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Undecided and data dependent two weeks before the September hike; no stated lean.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 'Do You Remember?'
items.quote: Put simply, the evolution of financial market structure leads to the evolution of how we carry out monetary policy effectively.
items.summary: Speech on monetary policy implementation: the ample-reserves framework, ON RRP and standing repo operations, and how tools must evolve with market structure (central clearing, stablecoins). No comment on the rate path or the economic outlook.
items.score_note: Implementation and market-structure speech with no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Opening remarks at the Philadelphia Fed 10th Annual Fintech Conference
items.quote: Looking ahead, if conditions evolve as I expect, some modest further tightening may be warranted.
items.summary: Paulson said she supported the 25bp hike at the September meeting because inflation risks were growing: underlying inflation is stuck at 2.5-3% and price pressure from the Middle East conflict and the AI buildout grew. She called returning inflation to 2% non-negotiable and said some modest further tightening may be warranted.
items.score_note: Conditional signal of modest further tightening ('may be warranted'); leaning tighter rather than calling for an immediate hike.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at a National Institute of Economic and Social Research conference, London
items.quote: likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year
items.summary: A week after the September hike, Williams described market forecasts that another hike may be appropriate by year-end and said that seems a reasonable way of thinking about it, while stressing the Fed will collect data as it did between July and September. He called inflation the big challenge and said it must return to 2% in a timely manner. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Endorses expectations of one more hike by year-end without committing to timing.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Panel discussion at a Cleveland Fed conference (with ECB and Bank of Mexico officials)
items.quote: the biggest risk with inflation is the formation of an inflationary mindset
items.summary: Hammack said the biggest inflation risk is an inflationary mindset forming after an extended period above target. FXStreet reports (paraphrase) that she said the Fed needs policy at a restrictive stance and that she does not see current policy restraining the economy. Reuters (via Kitco, same event) quoted her saying the rise in bond yields reflects real rates rather than inflation expectations, which remain reasonably well anchored, and paraphrased her as citing a solid outlook, competition for investor cash from strong tech-sector investment and repricing of the policy outlook.
items.score_note: Direct quote is about expectations risk; the call for a restrictive stance is only available as a paraphrase, so scored +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the University at Buffalo, 'Unwavering Dedication'
items.quote: one further upward adjustment of the federal funds target range may be appropriate late this year to support a timelier return of inflation to target
items.summary: Williams said inflation at 3.7% is unquestionably too high and the balance of risks has shifted toward price stability, citing AI-related demand and longer-lasting energy effects. After the September hike to 3.75-4.00% he sees no need for urgency, but one more hike late in 2026 may be appropriate if his forecast holds. He expects inflation at 3.5% this year and 2% in 2028.
items.score_note: Conditional, non-urgent guidance toward one more hike ('may be appropriate', 'no need for urgency'); leaning tighter rather than calling for an increase soon.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the 68th NABE annual meeting, Cleveland, 'Trimming the Sails: Communicating My Reaction Function'
items.quote: It reads, instead, as one that can handle a tighter hand on the tiller to finish the job on inflation.
items.summary: Hammack said a restrictive stance is needed for a timely return to 2% and that she sees financial conditions as neutral rather than restraining demand. She prefers frequent smaller adjustments made relatively quickly, sees inflation pressures as broad-based (energy, tariffs, AI-buildout demand) and upside risks dominant. Inflation above her forecast could require rates to go even higher; convincing labor deterioration would change the path.
items.score_note: Says policy is not yet restrictive and argues for further tightening through frequent smaller adjustments; language is metaphorical but the direction (more hikes needed) is explicit.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview with Reuters in Cleveland (same day as her NABE speech)
items.quote: I think we need to put more restriction in the economy.
items.summary: Hammack said rates need to move higher to restrain demand driven by corporate investment and wealth-effect consumption, hoping to cool inflation without raising unemployment above 4.2%. She said the timing is an open question and she would go to the October 27-28 meeting with an open mind. She worries an inflationary psychology is taking root as AI hyperscaler investment spills over to other firms.
items.score_note: States more restriction (higher rates) is needed; only the timing is open.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Interview with Bloomberg News (published October 13; reported by Reuters)
items.quote: I haven't changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike
items.summary: Williams reaffirmed that one more hike in 2026 may be appropriate and said he currently has no reason to believe more would be needed in 2027, though data could change that. He still sees disinflationary forces, expects inflation near 2% for 2027 as a whole, and said the economy is not overheating overall.
items.score_note: Still leans to one more hike this year but explicitly sees no need for further tightening in 2027; mild tightening lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at a Goldman Sachs event, New York
items.quote: I'm not feeling that there's restraint coming from financial conditions
items.summary: In one of the last appearances before the October blackout, Hammack said that if an inflationary mindset sets in, policy would have a harder job and the Fed might need to move even more. She said financial conditions seem roughly neutral, with technology investment going ahead despite higher borrowing costs. Reuters noted she gave no firm guidance on the October decision. The quote is a clause because the syndicated page contains hidden formatting characters in the longer sentences.
items.score_note: No restraint from financial conditions and a conditional warning of larger moves, but no explicit call for an October hike in the reported remarks; scored nearer zero than her October 12 remarks.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: FOMC meeting of October 27-28, 2026: dissent in favor of a 25bp increase (with Governor Cook)
items.quote: Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point
items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3.75-4.00%. Cook and Hammack voted against, preferring a 1/4 percentage point increase at this meeting. The quote is the vote line of the FOMC statement, not Hammack's own words. No separate dissent statement for this meeting was found in the Cleveland Fed speeches collection.
items.score_note: Formal dissent in favor of a rate increase.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Panel remarks at 'The SNB and Its Watchers' conference, Zurich, 'Reserve Currencies and Stablecoins'
items.quote: I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2 percent in a timely manner.
items.summary: In remarks mainly about safe-haven currencies and stablecoins, Hammack said inflation has moved in the wrong direction (headline PCE 3.6%, core 3.1% in September) and pressures are broad-based. She expects policy will need to move to a restrictive stance and prefers getting there through more frequent smaller adjustments to avoid falling behind.
items.score_note: States policy must still move to a restrictive stance, i.e. more hikes are needed, one week after dissenting for a hike.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at a European Central Bank conference, Frankfurt
items.quote: absolutely essential that we bring inflation back to our 2% target in a timely manner and a sustained basis
items.summary: Williams said US growth is resilient and the labor market remarkably stable, but inflation is absolutely too high and has been for too long. He said current shocks are not so far spilling into expectations or wages, did not discuss the next move, and said the last FOMC statement rightly concluded it was appropriate to collect more information. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Strong inflation language but no comment on the next move and an endorsement of gathering more information; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: 'Economic Outlook' speech at the Philadelphia Fed 81st Annual Field Meeting Capstone, Conshohocken, Pa.
items.quote: For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate.
items.summary: Paulson said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive, that she supported the September hike and the October hold, and that skipping a meeting is a matter of pace, not direction: there is likely more work to do. She prefers gradual tightening but would act more quickly if inflation expectations drift up, wage pressures build or underlying inflation moves higher. Underlying inflation is stuck at 2.5-3%.
items.score_note: States that further tightening is appropriate and that there is likely more work to do, which is an explicit call for more hikes, albeit at a gradual pace.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Conversation with Fisher College of Business students, Ohio State University
items.quote: My expectations are that we need to move to a restrictive stance of policy to help bring inflation back down to that 2% objective
items.summary: Hammack said policy needs to move to a restrictive stance or an inflationary mindset could take hold, with recent data moving in the wrong direction. She favors smaller, more frequent increases as less disruptive, does not think the Fed is behind the curve today, and would consider more aggressive moves only if it falls behind. She stressed these are conditional expectations, not forward guidance. (Reuters via Kitco.)
items.score_note: States that rates must still rise to a restrictive stance; favors steady 25bp steps over a larger move.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Panel at the UC Berkeley Alumni Salon, New York
items.quote: need to take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis
items.summary: Two days after a hot October CPI, Williams said the economy is strong, the labor market continues to strengthen and inflation is persistent, and that the Fed still has work to do to get policy to the right place. He gave no timing or size for further increases. He also said the Fed targets the inflation rate, not a reversal of the price level. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Says further policy actions are needed and that policy is not yet in the right place, i.e. more hikes are needed; no timing given.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview on Bloomberg TV
items.quote: I like moving in smaller increments
items.summary: Hammack repeated her preference for gradual, predictable rate increases and said larger increments are available if the Fed gets behind the curve. She said inflation pressures are broadening and financial conditions are not yet restrictive. Asked whether AI-related corporate borrowing is pushing up Treasury yields, she said that issuance is very small relative to government borrowing and attributed higher yields mainly to strong growth and expected Fed hikes. Reuters carried the same core quotes.
items.score_note: Continues to argue for further hikes (in 25bp steps) and says conditions are not yet restrictive.
items.ai_quote: While the scale of AI-related issuance is large for corporates, it’s very small relative to governments

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Keynote at the Brookings Institution on Treasury market resilience, 'Lessons from a Burning River'
items.quote: Finally, Fed communications should clearly distinguish policy actions from market-functioning actions.
items.summary: Speech on principles for Fed intervention in a stressed Treasury market: a high bar for intervention, temporary and targeted actions, enhancements to standing repo operations, and separate reporting of market-functioning purchases. The prepared text has no comment on the rate path.
items.score_note: Market-functioning and balance-sheet speech; no rate-path content in the prepared text.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: On-stage interview at the Axios BFD summit, New York
items.quote: If those continue, I think that's a factor that will argue that we may need to raise rates more
items.summary: Williams said the AI investment surge and stock-market wealth are strengthening the economy and, if they continue, may require raising rates more next year; AI is the more persistent inflation factor. He said the situation does not call for dramatic action, pushing back on a 50bp December move. He said the Fed is watching the fast-growing structured finance funding the AI boom but does not see a financial stability risk yet.
items.score_note: Conditional signal of more hikes ('may need to raise rates more') combined with a rejection of a larger step; lean tighter.
items.ai_quote: We are definitely seeing structured finance of the type we saw in housing finance, so that's why we're paying attention to that

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at Money Marketeers of New York University, 'Monetary Policy Communication: Do We Understand Each Other?'
items.quote: I see holding rates steady in October as a matter of pace, not direction
items.summary: A speech on Fed communication, reaction functions and credibility. In the text Paulson repeated that she supported the September hike and the October hold and that the pause was not a stop because markets expected further tightening. In the Q&A afterwards, as reported by Reuters (https://srnnews.com/feds-paulson-says-understanding-not-guidance-drives-effective-communication/), she said the way to bring inflation down is by having higher rates, that there is more tightening to do, and that slow and steady increases give the economy time to adjust.
items.score_note: The prepared text alone would be +1 (restates direction), but in the Q&A at the same event she said there is 'more tightening to do' (Reuters direct quote), which is an explicit statement that more hikes are needed. The machine-checkable quote is from the official text.

coverage_notes: Presidents confirmed on each bank's own site as of November 2026: John C. Williams (newyorkfed.org leadership page), Beth M. Hammack (clevelandfed.org profile and November 17 speech), Anna Paulson (philadelphiafed.org profile and November 19 speech). No change. Official texts: every Williams speech on the New York Fed speeches page in the window (June 25 Teller Window text, July 15, September 22, September 29), every Hammack entry in the Cleveland Fed speeches collection (June 2, July 31 statement, October 12, November 5, November 17) and every Paulson entry on the Philadelphia Fed speeches page (August 4 essay, September 24, November 10, November 19) were opened. Dissents: FOMC statements for June 17, July 29, September 16 and October 28 were opened. June and September had no dissents. July 29 was a hold with three dissents for a hike (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan); this July three-way dissent is not mentioned in the brief's context section. October 28 was 10-2 (Cook, Hammack). Hammack published a dissent statement for July (July 31) but no statement for the October dissent was found in the Cleveland Fed speeches collection or press releases. Williams and Paulson did not dissent at any of the four meetings. Hammack time_et values for speeches come from the speechTime field in the Cleveland Fed speeches listing; FOMC statement times are the stated 2:00 p.m. release. Thin coverage: Paulson has no items for June, July or October (no official text and no wire report with a direct quote was found; her first comment after the July FOMC was August 4). Williams has no August item other than the July 31 interview published August 3, and nothing found between October 13 and November 6. Bloomberg, WSJ, CNBC, MNI and Reuters originals were mostly paywalled or blocked, so wire remarks are sourced to syndicated copies (SRN News and Kitco for Reuters; Bloomberg Law, Fortune, The Standard for Bloomberg) and a few aggregator pages (briefs.co, ActionForex, FXStreet, qz.com).
